title: The training principles series: deloads
summary: He argues deloads are a strength-athlete tool that bodybuilders don't need. Complete time off is the worst option; a light low-volume deload is better but still recharges strength, which bodybuilders don't need to peak. Needing scheduled deloads signals poorly managed volume, intensity and frequency; he never deloads, only resting Sundays.

claims.claim: Taking a week or even 3-4 days fully off is a bad deload for bodybuilders; it may suit strength athletes recharging before competition.
Even when nursing most injuries it's better to move and get blood flowing; only a broken bone or torn tendon justifies not training, and that isn't a deload.
The objectively better deload is doing your usual lifts at low intensity and low volume, reducing tonnage while keeping blood flow and movement patterns so you don't need to relearn them.
Deloads exist to recharge strength so you can show max potential; bodybuilders aren't strength athletes, so that purpose doesn't apply.
If you need 3-4 days off every two months to keep progressing, your intensity or volume programming is wrong; frequency and recovery windows between days and body parts should always suffice.
A deload is either an emergency response to a programming mistake or, if scheduled, something that hurts your gains; focus on volume and intensity manipulation instead.
He never deloads; he rests only between body-part splits and takes Sundays fully off (no band work), which is more a mental and family recharge that makes him crave training.
He used to train seven days a week without problems or deloads; injuries from that period came from poor programming.
Stalled gains, tendinitis and similar issues trace back to poor programming: badly managed volume and intensity and poorly thought-out frequency.
Deload phases are boring because you don't push your limits, only to bring back strength you won't test.
Strength should trend steadily upward; if strength or tonnage drops unexpectedly, check your diet before deloading, since you may not be eating what you think.
